issue.title: VS2013 warning C4316 object allocated on the heap may not be aligned 16

body:
Is your code throwing an ERROR or a WARNING (based on the posts, I assume it's a warning, thus not a failure to compile)?  The SSE Specification prefers 16-byte alignment for optimum performance.  This is not a "bug" in the software, it is a design limitation of the hardware.  For more information read the following: https://software.intel.com/en-us/node/532814
If you are not using SSE calls on the struct then you can safely ignore the compiler warning.   As for the inability to allocate a struct on the heap, ~~can you post the code you are having issues with?  It would be easier to test.~~  the warning is valid.  What is happening is the C++ new operator is calling Windows API functions to allocate memory on the Heap.  These functions are not guaranteed to produce aligned memory accesses, and thus the compiler is notifying you of the situation.  As an alternative use the function _aligned_malloc() .  Marekkijo is correct.

references:
https://msdn.microsoft.com/en-us/library/y1w9bk0b.aspx
https://msdn.microsoft.com/en-us/library/83ythb65.aspx

body: This becomes tideous once you are working on a larger project in which a lot of these types are used across many classes. Overloading the new operator for every class allocated on the heap that has such a member requires a lot of extra code. Is there no "cleaner" solution to this?
What would help is a repro case as so far nobody provided any and I never been able to reproduce this bug.

This is NOT a bug, this issue needs to be closed.  As described above, the problem is not in the GLM library, but with other software using the GLM library improperly.  _aligned_malloc() MUST be used to guarantee proper structure alignment on the heap, or heap usage must be avoided.

If this is not a bug, as some are saying,  then the documentation needs to updated.

In order to use glm in a portable way, any c++ struct / class containing certain glm types must override the new operator. Bear in mind inheritance, and classes containing classes containing classes containing glm types.

Personally, in my humble opinion, this makes glm look really ugly.

In my humble opinion, I think that on platforms where malloc is not suitably aligned, and SSE is available and being used, classes like mat4 should internally aligned_malloc its SSE types.

For those who are concerned about a possible performance hit, perhaps we could add a glm::aligned::mat4 ??? Which would make the current assumptions.

Or, add glm::unaligned to detect and internally aligned_malloc its SSE types as mentioned previously.

But I certainly don't want to pass this alignment burden onto users of my code. It makes it harder to argue the case for switching to glm.

Just my humble opinion, thanks for listening.
